title: How do you do code / PR reviews (requirement, quality, business logic, exception handling, performance, security, tests, standards)?
shortTitle: How to do code / PR reviews

s1_definition.profdef: A code review, usually done on a pull request, is a structured evaluation of a proposed change by one or more engineers before it merges into the mainline. A thorough review checks that the change meets the requirement, is clean and maintainable, implements the business logic correctly, handles errors and edge cases, performs acceptably, is secure, is backed by adequate tests, and follows team standards. The goal is to catch defects early, share knowledge, and keep the codebase healthy, not to criticize the author.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of a code review as the supervisor sign-off before a large transaction is posted at National Bank of India. Before money moves, a second officer checks that the form matches what the customer asked for (requirement), is filled in neatly and legibly (quality), that the math is right (business logic), that it accounts for what happens if the account is frozen or overdrawn (exception handling), that it will not jam the queue at month-end (performance), that nobody can tamper with it (security), that there is a receipt and proof (tests), and that it follows the bank's standard procedure (standards). Only when all these pass does the transaction get posted.
s1_definition.oneliner: A good review verifies requirement, quality, correct business logic, error handling, performance, security, tests, and standards — catching defects early and spreading knowledge.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A code review, usually done on a pull request, is a structured evaluation of a proposed change by one or more engineers before it merges into the mainline. A thorough review checks that the change meets the requirement, is clean and maintainable, implements the business logic correctly, handles errors and edge cases, performs acceptably, is secure, is backed by adequate tests, and follows team standards. The goal is to catch defects early, share knowledge, and keep the codebase healthy, not to criticize the author.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of a code review as the supervisor sign-off before a large transaction is posted at National Bank of India. Before money moves, a second officer checks that the form matches what the customer asked for (requirement), is filled in neatly and legibly (quality), that the math is right (business logic), that it accounts for what happens if the account is frozen or overdrawn (exception handling), that it will not jam the queue at month-end (performance), that nobody can tamper with it (security), that there is a receipt and proof (tests), and that it follows the bank's standard procedure (standards). Only when all these pass does the transaction get posted.

**One line to remember:** A good review verifies requirement, quality, correct business logic, error handling, performance, security, tests, and standards — catching defects early and spreading knowledge.

sections.s2_technical:
The first thing I check is the requirement. Does this change actually do what the ticket asked, nothing less and nothing more. I read the ticket or user story first, then the pull request description, then the diff, confirming the scope matches. A change that solves a different problem, or sneaks in unrelated edits, is a red flag even if the code is good, because scope creep makes reviews and rollbacks harder. For a bank I also confirm the change does not quietly alter behavior outside what was requested.

Next is quality and maintainability. I look at naming — do method and variable names say what they mean — at function size and single responsibility, at duplication, and at readability. I ask whether a new engineer could understand this in six months. I prefer clear code over clever code. I check that the change fits the existing architecture rather than bolting on a new pattern inconsistently.

Then business logic correctness, which in banking is where real money is at stake. I trace the logic by hand against realistic cases: does the interest calculation round correctly, does the transfer debit and credit the right accounts, does it use BigDecimal and never floating point for money. I look hard at boundary conditions — zero amounts, exactly-at-the-limit values, negative inputs — because that is where financial bugs hide.

Exception handling is next. I check that errors are handled at the right level, that exceptions are specific rather than catching Throwable and swallowing it, that failures do not leave data half-written, and that transactions roll back cleanly on error. I verify that error messages do not leak sensitive data and that the code fails safe — for a bank, failing closed (rejecting) is usually safer than failing open (allowing).

Performance comes next, proportionate to the context. I look for obvious problems: N-plus-one database queries, unbounded loops over large data, missing indexes implied by a new query, holding locks or database connections too long, or doing expensive work inside a transaction. I do not demand premature micro-optimization, but I flag anything that will not scale to production volumes, like a report that loads every transaction into memory.

Security is critical in banking. I check for parameterized queries rather than string-concatenated SQL to prevent injection, proper input validation, correct authorization checks so a user cannot act on another account, no secrets hardcoded in the code, sensitive data encrypted and not logged, and safe handling of untrusted input. A single security gap in a bank can mean real financial loss, so this is never skipped.

Tests are the evidence the change works. I confirm there are unit tests for the new logic, that they cover the happy path and the important failure and boundary cases, that they actually assert meaningful outcomes rather than just running, and that they are deterministic. If a bug is being fixed, I want a test that would have caught it. Finally, standards: formatting, linting, commit message conventions, documentation of public APIs, and consistency with team practices. A senior-level nuance I always mention is the human side — I phrase comments as questions and suggestions, distinguish blocking issues from nitpicks, praise good work, and review promptly so I do not block teammates. The review is about the code, never the person, and a healthy review culture is one of the strongest quality tools a team has.
sections.s3_banking:
A National Bank of India engineer opens a pull request adding a withdrawal feature, and I review it against all the dimensions.

Problem 1 — the first PR concatenated user input straight into a SQL string and used double for the balance. This is exactly why security and business-logic review matter — the injection risk and the floating-point money bug must be caught before merge.

Problem 2 — the code caught a broad Exception and logged the full account number, and it had no test for an overdraft. This is exactly why exception-handling and test review matter — swallowing errors, leaking PII, and missing boundary tests are blocking issues in a bank.

Problem 3 — the method loaded every transaction into memory to compute a balance. This is exactly why performance review matters — it would not scale to a real account's history.

The mini-project shows a before version with these defects and an after version that passes review, plus a short review checklist as comments. The WithdrawalService Java class is the real code under review.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
accounts-service/
└── src/
    ├── main/java/com/bank/accounts/
    │   ├── WithdrawalService.java        (the code under review)
    │   └── AccountRepository.java
    └── test/java/com/bank/accounts/

```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# A reviewer runs these BEFORE approving — CI runs them on the PR too.
mvn clean test              # all tests must pass
mvn verify                  # coverage + integration gates

# Static analysis / security scan commonly wired into the PR pipeline.
mvn spotbugs:check          # finds bug patterns
mvn dependency-check:check  # flags vulnerable dependencies

# Review the exact diff the PR proposes.
git diff origin/main...feature/withdrawal
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a pull request adding a withdrawal feature, submitted with the defective version, flows through my review.

Step 1: I read the ticket, then the PR description, then the diff. The ticket asked only for a guarded withdrawal. I confirm scope: the change does what was asked and contains no unrelated edits. Requirement check passes.

Step 2: I read for quality. The method is small and the intent is clear after revision, names are meaningful, and it uses constructor injection so it is testable. Quality check passes on the revised version.

Step 3: I trace the business logic by hand. Withdrawing 50000 from Rajesh's 1000000 yields 950000, computed with BigDecimal, and an overdraft is rejected. I specifically test the boundary where the amount equals the balance. Business-logic check passes.

Step 4: I check exception handling and security. The revised code throws specific exceptions, rolls back the transaction on failure, fails closed on overdraft, and the repository uses parameterized queries so injection is impossible, with no PII logged. These blocking issues from the first version are resolved.

Step 5: I check performance — the balance comes from a single indexed lookup, not loading all transactions into memory — and tests, confirming the suite covers the happy path, the overdraft boundary, and invalid input with meaningful assertions. Performance and test checks pass.

Step 6: I check standards — formatting, naming conventions, and a clear ticket-linked commit message — leave a couple of non-blocking suggestions phrased as questions, approve, and the PR merges once CI is green. The defective version would have been blocked on security, money math, exception handling, and missing tests.

```
Oct 25, 2026 05:00:02 AM INFO: review: requirement matches ticket, scope clean
Oct 25, 2026 05:05:11 AM SEVERE: v1 BLOCKING: SQL injection + double for money
Oct 25, 2026 05:06:40 AM SEVERE: v1 BLOCKING: broad catch, PII logged, no tests
Oct 25, 2026 05:20:03 AM INFO: v2: parameterized queries, BigDecimal, fail-closed overdraft
Oct 25, 2026 05:22:22 AM INFO: v2: tests cover happy + boundary + invalid; CI green
Oct 25, 2026 05:23:00 AM INFO: approved + merged
```

```
  Pull Request opened (withdrawal feature)
    │
    ▼
  REVIEW CHECKLIST (each dimension):
    ├─ Requirement      : matches ticket? scope clean?        ✓
    ├─ Quality          : names, size, readability            ✓
    ├─ Business logic    : BigDecimal, boundaries, correctness ✓
    ├─ Exception handling: specific, rollback, fail-closed     ✓
    ├─ Performance       : no N+1, no load-all-into-memory      ✓
    ├─ Security          : parameterized SQL, authz, no secrets ✓
    ├─ Tests             : happy + boundary + failure asserted  ✓
    └─ Standards         : format, lint, commit message         ✓
    │
    ├─ any BLOCKING issue ─▶ request changes ─▶ author pushes fixes ─┐
    │                                                                │
    ▼ all pass + CI green                                            │
  Approve ─▶ merge to main ◀───────────────────────────────────────┘
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Review Dimensions as a Structured Gate ═══

  ┌─ Review Checklist (blocking vs nitpick) ─────────────────────┐
  │  Requirement       : scope matches ticket        [blocking]  │
  │  Quality           : names/size/duplication       [mostly nit]│
  │  Business logic     : BigDecimal, boundaries       [blocking]  │
  │  Exception handling : specific, rollback, fail-safe[blocking]  │
  │  Performance        : N+1, memory, locks           [blocking]  │
  │  Security           : injection, authz, secrets    [blocking]  │
  │  Tests              : happy+boundary+failure        [blocking]  │
  │  Standards          : format/lint/commit msg        [nitpick]   │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Before vs After (what review fixes) ────────────────────

  BEFORE                          AFTER
  ──────                          ─────
  string-concat SQL   ──fix──▶    parameterized (?) query
  double balance      ──fix──▶    BigDecimal money
  throws Exception    ──fix──▶    specific exceptions + rollback
  log full account #  ──fix──▶    no PII logged
  no tests            ──fix──▶    happy + boundary + failure tests

  ── State Diagram: PR Review ───────────────────────────────

  [OPEN] ──reviewer reads──→ [CHANGES_REQUESTED] ──author fixes──→ [RE-REVIEW]
     │                                                               │
     │                         all dimensions pass + CI green        │
     └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────── ▼
                                                                  [APPROVED] ──▶ [MERGED]

  ── Call Chain (review flow) ───────────────────────────────

  1. read ticket -> PR description -> diff   (requirement + scope)
  2. assess quality/readability
  3. trace business logic by hand            (money math, boundaries)
  4. check exceptions + security             (blocking gates)
  5. check performance + tests
  6. check standards; comment; approve/request changes
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
When I review a pull request I work through a consistent set of dimensions rather than just skimming the diff. I start with the requirement — I read the ticket, then the PR description, then the code, and confirm the change does exactly what was asked, nothing less and nothing more, because unrelated scope creep makes reviews and rollbacks harder. Then I assess quality and maintainability: meaningful names, small single-purpose methods, no needless duplication, and code a new engineer could understand in six months.

Next I verify the business logic by tracing it by hand against realistic cases, which in banking is where real money is at stake. I confirm money uses BigDecimal and never floating point, and I look hard at boundary conditions like zero, exactly-at-the-limit, and negative values, because that is where financial bugs hide. Then exception handling: specific exceptions rather than swallowing a broad catch, clean transaction rollback on failure, failing closed so an error rejects rather than allows, and no sensitive data leaked in error messages or logs.

I then check performance proportionate to context — watching for N-plus-one queries, loading large data into memory, or holding locks and connections too long — and security, which is never optional in a bank: parameterized queries to prevent SQL injection, proper input validation and authorization so a user cannot act on another account, and no hardcoded secrets. After that I check the tests, confirming they cover the happy path plus the important failure and boundary cases with meaningful assertions, and if it is a bug fix, that there is a test which would have caught the bug. Finally I check standards — formatting, linting, commit conventions, and documentation.

At National Bank of India I once reviewed a withdrawal feature whose first version concatenated user input into SQL, used double for the balance, caught a broad exception while logging the full account number, and had no tests. I blocked it on security, money math, exception handling, and missing tests, and the revised version used parameterized queries, BigDecimal, specific exceptions with rollback, a fail-closed overdraft check, and a proper test suite. Throughout, I keep the review about the code and never the person — I phrase comments as questions, separate blocking issues from nitpicks, praise good work, and review promptly so I never block the team. A healthy review culture is one of the strongest quality tools a team has.
